steps.eyebrow: Browser same-origin policy and the CORS/authentication boundary
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: For a browser page calling an API, separate address matching from permission to access the endpoint.
An origin combines scheme, host and port. A difference in any one makes URLs cross-origin.
Browser restrictions limit a script’s access to cross-origin responses unless the server permits it through CORS. The API must independently check endpoint access.
https://shop.example:443/orders and https://shop.example:443/items share an origin despite different paths. Changing the host to api.example or the port to 8443 makes the call cross-origin.
Browser permission to read a response is not authentication. The API still needs its own access checks.

public.prompt: A script at https://shop.example calls https://api.example. CORS permits reading the response. What follows for endpoint access checks?

options.text: The API must still check access independently of CORS.
CORS permission replaces endpoint access checks.
The browser's origin restriction itself authenticates the caller.

option1.message: Correct: The API must still check access independently of CORS.

option2.message: CORS concerns browser response access, not the API's independent access checks.

option3.message: A browser restriction is not an endpoint access check.

correct.message: The API must still check access independently of CORS.

incorrect.message: Recheck the taught rule and the specific evidence. Read the explanation for the selected option.

public.prompt: Classify each browser-page URL relative to the fixed API https://shop.example:443/orders. Identify the differing origin component; a path difference alone is not an origin difference.

item1.message: Origin comparison: same-origin; differing component: none.

item2.message: Origin comparison: cross-origin; differing component: scheme.

item3.message: Origin comparison: cross-origin; differing component: host.

item4.message: Origin comparison: cross-origin; differing component: port.

correct.message: Each judgement follows the specific evidence in its excerpt or URL, not a package name, response alone or an unrelated permission.

incorrect.message: Recheck the taught rule and the specific evidence. A browser origin is the combination of scheme, host and port; a difference in any of these makes two URLs cross-origin.

hints: Compare each URL’s scheme, host and port with the fixed API. Ignore path differences.

blocks.text: Choose an order operation’s method by its intended effect, not by a convenient label.
Safe methods request essentially read-only semantics. Incidental logging does not make them unsafe.

Idempotency means identical repetition has the same intended server effect as one request, even if replies differ. GET retrieves a representation; HEAD has the same semantics without response content. Both are safe and idempotent. POST requests resource-specific processing and is not generally idempotent. PUT creates or replaces target state; DELETE removes its association with current functionality. Both are idempotent, not safe.

left.alt_text: GET retrieves a representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without response content; both map to safe and idempotent.

nodes.label: PUT: create or replace target state
POST: resource-specific processing; not generally idempotent

right.alt_text: PUT creates or replaces target state and DELETE removes its association; both map to idempotent, not safe. POST requests resource-specific processing and is not generally idempotent.

blocks.takeaway: Safety and idempotency are separate properties.

blocks.text: Reading an order and replacing it can both be idempotent, but only reading is safe. Repeated PUT requests the same target state; POST processing is not generally idempotent. Describe the requested change and identical repetition separately. Matching replies are not the test.

At /orders/42, GET retrieves a representation and HEAD requests the same semantics without content. Logging is incidental. Repeating a PUT replacement requests the same target state, even if replies differ. Repeated DELETE also need not return identical replies. POST collection processing is not generally idempotent. Ask separately: does this request a change, and does identical repetition preserve the intended effect?
Safety does not prohibit all incidental effects. Idempotency does not require identical replies. PUT and DELETE can be idempotent yet unsafe.

public.prompt: A GET retrieves an order and writes an incidental log entry; a PUT replaces that order's state. Which safety/idempotency judgement is correct?

options.text: PUT is safe because repeating it has the same intended effect.
GET remains safe and idempotent; PUT is idempotent but not safe.
Both are unsafe because both can write something.

option1.message: Idempotency does not imply read-only requested semantics.

option2.message: Correct: GET remains safe and idempotent; PUT is idempotent but not safe.

option3.message: Safety concerns requested semantics; incidental retrieval logging does not make GET unsafe.

correct.message: GET remains safe and idempotent; PUT is idempotent but not safe.

incorrect.message: Recheck the taught rule and the specific evidence. Read the explanation for the selected option.

hints: Separate the roles named in the prompt; apply the taught distinction rather than treating them as interchangeable.

public.prompt: For each orders operation, choose its method and safety/idempotency judgement. Repetition means identical requests and intended server effect, not identical response messages.

items.text: Retrieve the selected order representation. The server also writes an incidental retrieval log.
Request the same retrieval semantics but no response content.
Process submitted content to create a new order, without any additional idempotency guarantee.
Create or replace the state of the known target /orders/42. Repeated identical requests need not have identical responses.
Remove the association of /orders/42 with its current functionality. A later identical request may have a different response.

item1.message: GET retrieves; incidental logging remains compatible with safety.

item2.message: HEAD has retrieval semantics without response content; it is safe and idempotent.

item3.message: POST requests resource-specific processing and is not generally idempotent.

item4.message: PUT creates or replaces target state; idempotency concerns intended effects rather than response equality.

item5.message: DELETE is idempotent but not safe; differing responses do not disprove equal intended effects.

correct.message: Each judgement follows the specific evidence in its excerpt or URL, not a package name, response alone or an unrelated permission.

incorrect.message: Recheck the taught rule and the specific evidence. A safe method has essentially read-only requested semantics; incidental effects such as logging do not make it unsafe.

hints: Identify the requested operation first. Then judge read-only semantics and the intended effect of identical repetition separately.

blocks.text: An order’s outgoing body format, preferred response format and actual response format are separate information.
Content-Type labels the media type of its associated representation, not the preferred response format.

Accept lists acceptable response media types. For JSON content, send Content-Type: application/json; request a JSON response with Accept: application/json. Inspect the reply’s Content-Type separately.
In this JSON exchange, the request Content-Type labels the submitted content. Accept states the response preference. Read the response’s own Content-Type to identify what came back.
Content-Type labels content. Accept carries the client’s response preference.

left.alt_text: POST /orders HTTP/1.1 → Host: shop.example → Content-Type: application/json → Accept: application/json → {"quantity": 3}

blocks.left_label: Request: body label and response preference

public.prompt: A JSON request sends Content-Type: application/json and Accept: application/json. Which header identifies the media type actually returned?

option1.message: Accept communicates acceptable response formats, not the returned representation's metadata.

option2.message: That Content-Type describes the outgoing JSON content, not the response content.

incorrect.message: Recheck the taught rule and the specific evidence. Read the explanation for the selected option.
